title: Groups of Special-Equivalent Strings
statement:
You get an array `words` of lowercase strings that all have the same length. One move on a string swaps two of its characters whose indices are both even, or two whose indices are both odd (indices start at 0). Two strings are special-equivalent when some number of moves (zero or more) applied to the first one makes it identical to the second.

Special-equivalence splits `words` into groups: inside a group every two strings are special-equivalent, and no string outside the group is special-equivalent to its members. Return the number of groups. Identical strings at different positions fall into the same group.
constraints: words[i] contains only lowercase English letters
All strings in words have the same length
notes:
## Intuition

Moves can rearrange the even-index letters in any order and the odd-index letters in any order, but a letter can never cross from an even index to an odd one. So two words are special-equivalent exactly when they have the same multiset of letters at even indices and the same multiset at odd indices. Counting each letter separately for the two kinds of index gives a fingerprint that is equal for equivalent words and different otherwise, and the answer is the number of distinct fingerprints. (A slower check sorts both halves of every word and compares each word with one member of every group found so far.)

## Approach

1. Keep a set `groups` of fingerprints.
2. For each `word`, make `count` with 52 slots: slots 0–25 count letters at even indices, slots 26–51 count letters at odd indices.
3. For each index `i`, turn the character into `letter` (0 for `a`) and add one to slot `letter + 26 * (i % 2)`.
4. Join `count` into a string and add it to `groups`.
5. Return the size of `groups`.

## Example 1, step by step

- `"abcd"`: even indices hold `a, c`, odd hold `b, d`. `"cdab"` (even `c, a`, odd `d, b`) and `"cbad"` (even `c, a`, odd `b, d`) give the same counts, so all three share one fingerprint.
- `"xyzz"`: even `x, z`, odd `y, z`; `"zzxy"` has even `z, x`, odd `z, y`, the same fingerprint.
- `"zzyx"`: even `z, y`, odd `z, x`, a new fingerprint.
- `groups` ends with 3 entries, so the answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · (L + 52)): each word of length L is counted once and its 52 counts are joined.
- Space: O(n) fingerprints of 52 numbers each in the worst case.

## Pitfalls

- Sorting or counting the whole word is not enough: `"ab"` and `"ba"` contain the same letters but are in different groups.
- Join the counts with a separator; without one, counts like `1, 11` and `11, 1` produce the same string.
- Duplicate words are the same group, not separate ones; a set handles this automatically.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `groups` | set of distinct fingerprints seen so far |
| `word` | the string being fingerprinted |
| `count` | 26 counts for even indices followed by 26 for odd indices |
| `i` | index of the current character in `word` |
| `letter` | the character as 0 to 25 |

narration.2: Each distinct fingerprint stands for one group, so a set collects them.
narration.4: Slots 0-25 will count even-index letters and slots 26-51 odd-index letters.
narration.5: Visit every character of the word with its index.
narration.6: Turn the character into a number from 0 for a to 25 for z.
narration.7: Count it on the even side or the odd side, depending on the parity of its index.
narration.9: Equivalent words have identical counts, so the joined counts identify the group.
narration.11: The number of distinct fingerprints is the number of groups.
